title: Gram–Schmidt, QR, least squares, inner product spaces
summary: Gram–Schmidt turns any basis into an orthogonal one (and gives A = QR); least squares finds the best approximate solution of an inconsistent system through the normal equations AᵀAx̂ = Aᵀb. The same projection ideas work in any inner product space, including polynomials and functions.

blocks.name: Gram–Schmidt
blocks.text: Given a basis {x₁, …, xₚ} of W, define v₁ = x₁, v₂ = x₂ − ((x₂·v₁)/(v₁·v₁))v₁, and in general vₖ = xₖ − (projection of xₖ onto Span{v₁, …, vₖ₋₁}). Then {v₁, …, vₚ} is an orthogonal basis of W, and Span{v₁, …, vₖ} = Span{x₁, …, xₖ} for every k.

proof.text: Each vₖ is xₖ minus its projection onto Wₖ₋₁ = Span{v₁, …, vₖ₋₁}, so by the orthogonal decomposition theorem it is orthogonal to Wₖ₋₁, i.e. to all earlier v's. It is nonzero because xₖ ∉ Wₖ₋₁ (the x's are independent). The projection formula is valid because the earlier v's are already orthogonal.

blocks.text: Why subtract projections onto the earlier vectors: what remains of xₖ after removing everything that points along the directions already chosen is exactly the new, perpendicular direction. You must project onto the new v's (which are orthogonal), not the old x's.
You may rescale any vₖ (e.g. clear fractions) before continuing; it changes neither the span nor later projections. Normalize at the end to get an orthonormal basis.

blocks.title: Gram–Schmidt in ℝ³
blocks.prompt: Apply Gram–Schmidt to x₁ = (1, 1, 0), x₂ = (1, 0, 1), x₃ = (0, 1, 1), then normalize.

blocks.name: Why vₖ is orthogonal to v₁ (the key computation)
blocks.text: With v₂ = x₂ − (x₂·v₁/v₁·v₁)v₁: v₂·v₁ = x₂·v₁ − (x₂·v₁/v₁·v₁)(v₁·v₁) = x₂·v₁ − x₂·v₁ = 0. The same one-line computation, using that the earlier v's are mutually orthogonal, shows vₖ·vⱼ = 0 for every j < k.

blocks.title: Gram–Schmidt with ∫₋₁¹: the first Legendre polynomials (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: Orthogonalize 1, t, t² in ℙ₂ with ⟨f, g⟩ = ∫₋₁¹ f(t)g(t) dt, and give ‖·‖² of each result.

blocks.text: Symmetric intervals plus parity save almost all the integration: odd·even integrands vanish on [−a, a].

blocks.name: QR factorization
blocks.text: If A is m×n with linearly independent columns, A = QR where Q is m×n with orthonormal columns forming a basis of Col A, and R is n×n upper triangular, invertible, with positive diagonal.

proof.text: Gram–Schmidt (normalized) on the columns of A gives Q. Since Span{q₁, …, qₖ} = Span{a₁, …, aₖ}, each aₖ is a combination of q₁, …, qₖ only, so the coefficient matrix R is upper triangular. Multiply A = QR on the left by Qᵀ and use QᵀQ = I: R = QᵀA.

blocks.title: Find QR
items: Gram–Schmidt on the columns of A; normalize to get the columns of Q.
Compute R = QᵀA (entries are dot products qᵢ·aⱼ; below-diagonal ones are 0).
Check: diagonal of R positive; QR = A.

blocks.title: QR of a 3×2 matrix
blocks.prompt: Find a QR factorization of A = [1 4; 2 5; 2 2].

blocks.title: QR in ℝ⁴ and least squares through it (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: A = [1 3; 1 1; 1 1; 1 −1]. Find A = QR and use it to solve the least-squares problem for b = (1, 2, 3, 4).
steps: Back-substitute: 2√2·x̂₂ = −3/√2 ⇒ x̂₂ = −3/4; 2x̂₁ + 2x̂₂ = 5 ⇒ x̂₁ = 13/4. (Same as solving AᵀAx̂ = Aᵀb.)

blocks.text: Why QR helps numerically: AᵀA squares the condition number of A, while Rx̂ = Qᵀb works with A's own conditioning. On exams, QR mostly saves you from inverting AᵀA: R is triangular, so back-substitution suffices.
For an (often inconsistent) system Ax = b, x̂ is a least-squares solution if ‖b − Ax̂‖ ≤ ‖b − Ax‖ for all x. The number ‖b − Ax̂‖ is the least-squares error.

blocks.name: Normal equations
blocks.text: The least-squares solutions of Ax = b are exactly the solutions of AᵀAx = Aᵀb. Equivalently, Ax̂ = b̂ = projCol A b.

proof.text: Ax ranges over Col A, so the closest Ax to b is b̂ = projCol A b (best approximation). The error b − Ax̂ must be orthogonal to Col A, i.e. to every column of A: Aᵀ(b − Ax̂) = 0, which is AᵀAx̂ = Aᵀb. The steps reverse.

blocks.title: Least squares by normal equations
items: Solve AᵀAx̂ = Aᵀb (row reduce, or invert if 2×2).

blocks.title: Least squares via the normal equations
blocks.prompt: Find the least-squares solution and error for A = [4 0; 0 2; 1 1], b = (2, 0, 11).

blocks.name: Least squares with QR
blocks.text: If A = QR (independent columns), the unique least-squares solution is x̂ = R⁻¹Qᵀb; in practice solve Rx̂ = Qᵀb by back-substitution.

proof.text: Qᵀb gives the coordinates of b̂ = QQᵀb in the basis Q, and Ax = QRx = b̂ ⇔ Rx = Qᵀb.

blocks.title: Least squares via QR
blocks.prompt: With A = [1 4; 2 5; 2 2] = QR as above, find the least-squares solution of Ax = (1, 2, 3).
steps: Back-substitute Rx̂ = Qᵀb with R = [3 6; 0 3]: 3x̂₂ = −2/3 ⇒ x̂₂ = −2/9.

blocks.text: If the columns of A are orthogonal, AᵀA is diagonal and x̂ⱼ = (b·aⱼ)/(aⱼ·aⱼ): just projection coefficients.

blocks.title: Least squares with orthogonal columns (exam-hard shortcut)
blocks.prompt: Solve the least-squares problem for A = [1 −1; 1 1; 1 1; 1 −1], b = (1, 2, 4, 3), and find the error.
steps: The columns a₁ = (1, 1, 1, 1), a₂ = (−1, 1, 1, −1) are orthogonal (dot product 0), so AᵀA = diag(4, 4).

blocks.text: Interpretation: b̂ = Ax̂ is the point of Col A closest to b, the residual b − Ax̂ is orthogonal to every column, and the least-squares error is the distance from b to Col A. If b is already in Col A the error is 0 and the least-squares solutions are the ordinary solutions.

blocks.name: When is x̂ unique?
blocks.text: TFAE: (a) AᵀAx = Aᵀb has a unique solution for every b; (b) the columns of A are linearly independent; (c) AᵀA is invertible. Then x̂ = (AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀb.

proof.text: Nul(AᵀA) = Nul A: if AᵀAx = 0, then 0 = xᵀAᵀAx = ‖Ax‖², so Ax = 0. So AᵀA (square) is invertible ⇔ Nul A = {0}.

blocks.text: If the columns are dependent there are infinitely many least-squares solutions (a translate of Nul A), but b̂ = Ax̂ is still unique. Example: A = [1 1 2; 1 −1 0; 1 1 2; 1 −1 0] has column 3 = column 1 + column 2, so its least-squares solutions form a line.
Fit y = β₀ + β₁x to data (x₁, y₁), …, (xₙ, yₙ): design matrix X with rows (1, xᵢ), parameter vector β = (β₀, β₁), observation vector y. Solve XᵀXβ = Xᵀy. XᵀX = [n Σxᵢ; Σxᵢ Σxᵢ²], Xᵀy = (Σyᵢ, Σxᵢyᵢ).

blocks.title: Set up a curve fit (do not solve)
blocks.prompt: Set up the least-squares problem for fitting y = β₀ + β₁x + β₂x² to (−1, 2), (0, 1), (1, 1), (2, 4).
steps: Each data point gives one equation β₀ + β₁xᵢ + β₂xᵢ² = yᵢ.
Design matrix rows (1, xᵢ, xᵢ²): X = [1 −1 1; 1 0 0; 1 1 1; 1 2 4].
blocks.answer: X = [1 −1 1; 1 0 0; 1 1 1; 1 2 4], y = (2, 1, 1, 4), normal equations XᵀXβ = Xᵀy.

blocks.title: Quadratic fit, fully solved (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: Fit y = β₀ + β₁x + β₂x² to (−1, 2), (0, 1), (1, 1), (2, 4) by least squares.
steps: XᵀX = [4 2 6; 2 6 8; 6 8 18] (sums of 1, x, x², x³, x⁴), Xᵀy = (Σy, Σxy, Σx²y) = (8, 7, 19).
Row reduce [XᵀX | Xᵀy] to get β = (7/10, −2/5, 1).
Fitted values at x = −1, 0, 1, 2: 2.1, 0.7, 1.3, 3.9, close to the data.

blocks.title: Uniqueness with a parameter
blocks.prompt: For which h does Ax = b have a unique least-squares solution for every b, where A = [1 2; 2 h; 3 6]?
steps: Unique ⇔ columns independent. Column 2 = 2·column 1 exactly when h = 4.
For h ≠ 4 the columns are independent ⇒ AᵀA invertible ⇒ unique x̂.

blocks.text: A function ⟨u, v⟩ on a vector space V with: (1) ⟨u, v⟩ = ⟨v, u⟩; (2) ⟨u + v, w⟩ = ⟨u, w⟩ + ⟨v, w⟩; (3) ⟨cu, v⟩ = c⟨u, v⟩; (4) ⟨u, u⟩ ≥ 0, and ⟨u, u⟩ = 0 only for u = 0. Length, distance, orthogonality, projections and Gram–Schmidt are then defined exactly as in ℝⁿ.

items: Evaluation inner product on ℙₙ: ⟨p, q⟩ = p(t₀)q(t₀) + ⋯ + p(tₖ)q(tₖ) with DISTINCT points; it is an inner product iff k + 1 ≥ n + 1 points (a nonzero p of degree ≤ n cannot vanish at n + 1 points).
Integral inner product on C[a, b]: ⟨f, g⟩ = ∫ₐᵇ f(t)g(t) dt. Then ‖f‖² = ∫ₐᵇ f(t)² dt.

blocks.name: Cauchy–Schwarz and triangle inequalities
blocks.text: |⟨u, v⟩| ≤ ‖u‖‖v‖ and ‖u + v‖ ≤ ‖u‖ + ‖v‖ in every inner product space.

proof.text: If u ≠ 0, the projection of v onto u has length |⟨v, u⟩|/‖u‖, which is at most ‖v‖ by Pythagoras.

blocks.title: Check the axioms
blocks.prompt: Is ⟨p, q⟩ = p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1) an inner product on ℙ₂? Is ⟨x, y⟩ = x₁y₁ + 2x₂y₂ one on ℝ²?
steps: Symmetry and linearity hold for both (evaluation and multiplication are linear).
ℙ₂ case: p = t(t − 1) = t² − t is nonzero but p(0) = p(1) = 0, so ⟨p, p⟩ = 0. Axiom 4 fails.
ℝ² case: ⟨x, x⟩ = x₁² + 2x₂² > 0 unless x = 0. All four axioms hold.
blocks.answer: First: no (positivity fails for t² − t). Second: yes.

blocks.title: Norm and best approximation in C[0, 1]
blocks.prompt: With ⟨f, g⟩ = ∫₀¹ fg dt, find ‖t‖ and the best approximation to t² by a polynomial of degree ≤ 1.
steps: Use the orthogonal basis {1, t − 1/2} of ℙ₁ from the previous example.

blocks.text: Orthogonality depends on the inner product: 1 and t are orthogonal for ∫₋₁¹ but not for ∫₀¹.

blocks.title: Which formulas define inner products? (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: (a) ⟨x, y⟩ = x₁y₁ − x₂y₂ on ℝ². (b) ⟨p, q⟩ = p(0)q(0) + p′(0)q′(0) + p″(0)q″(0) on ℙ₂. (c) Compute ‖sin t‖ in C[0, π] with ⟨f, g⟩ = ∫₀^π fg dt.
steps: (b) Symmetric and linear (evaluation and differentiation are linear). Positivity: for p = a + bt + ct², ⟨p, p⟩ = a² + b² + (2c)², which is 0 only if a = b = c = 0. Yes, an inner product.
(c) ‖sin t‖² = ∫₀^π sin²t dt = π/2, so ‖sin t‖ = √(π/2).

blocks.text: All of this unit is one idea used four ways: the closest point of a subspace W to a vector y is its orthogonal projection, and projections are easy once W has an orthogonal basis.

hard.title: True/False: QR, least squares, inner products

items: 1. If A = QR where Q has orthonormal columns, then R = QᵀA.
2. The least-squares solution of Ax = b is unique.
3. If b ∈ Col A, every least-squares solution is an exact solution.
4. ⟨p, q⟩ = p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1) is an inner product on ℙ₂.
5. In Gram–Schmidt, Span{v₁, …, vₖ} = Span{x₁, …, xₖ} for every k.
6. |⟨u, v⟩| ≤ ‖u‖‖v‖ holds in every inner product space.
2. False. Unique ⇔ columns of A independent. With dependent columns there are infinitely many.
3. True. Then b̂ = b, and LS solutions are the solutions of Ax = b̂.
4. False. p = t(t − 1) ≠ 0 has ⟨p, p⟩ = 0. Positivity fails: need at least 3 evaluation points for ℙ₂.
5. True. Each vₖ is xₖ minus a combination of earlier v’s, and vice versa.

solution.text: What it tests: LS uniqueness ⇔ AᵀA invertible ⇔ independent columns. An inner product must be positive on every nonzero vector.

solution.title: Solution
items: Column 3 = column 1 + column 2, so LS solutions are not unique. Col A = Span{a₁, a₂}, and a₁·a₂ = 0.
x̂ = (3, −1, 0) + t(−1, −1, 1), t ∈ ℝ. (AᵀA has rank 2, so the normal equations have one free variable — same answer.)

solution.text: What it tests: Dependent columns ⇒ a whole line of LS solutions; b̂ is still unique. Using an orthogonal basis of Col A avoids solving a singular 3×3 system.

prompt.text: On ℙ₂ use ⟨p, q⟩ = p(−1)q(−1) + p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1). (a) Orthogonalize 1, t, t². (b) Find the best approximation to t³ in ℙ₁ (polynomials of degree ≤ 1) and explain why it’s so good.

solution.title: Solution
items: Error t³ − t vanishes at −1, 0, 1, so its norm in this inner product is 0 — on the three sample points the approximation is exact.

solution.text: What it tests: An evaluation inner product only “sees” the sample points. Orthogonality depends on the inner product — 1 and t² are not orthogonal here.

prompt.text: With ⟨f, g⟩ = ∫₋₁¹ fg dt, find the best approximation to t³ by polynomials of degree ≤ 1, and then by degree ≤ 2. Why are they equal?

solution.title: Solution
items: ⟨t³, t² − 1/3⟩ = ∫(t⁵ − t³/3) = 0 (odd integrand). So degree ≤ 2 gives the same (3/5)t: t³ is odd and the new basis vector is even.

solution.text: What it tests: Odd × even integrates to 0 on symmetric intervals — saves almost all integration. The answer is not t (t is the answer for a three-point evaluation inner product, not this one).

prompt.text: Prove: AᵀA is invertible if and only if the columns of A are linearly independent.

solution.title: Solution
items: AᵀA is square, so invertible ⇔ Nul(AᵀA) = {0} ⇔ Nul A = {0} ⇔ independent columns. ∎

solution.text: What it tests: The trick is multiplying by xᵀ to create a squared length. Also gives rank(AᵀA) = rank A.

hard.title: Build an inner product with prescribed orthogonality

prompt.text: Find a symmetric matrix M so that ⟨x, y⟩ = xᵀMy is an inner product on ℝ² in which (1, 0) and (1, 1) are orthogonal. Verify positivity.

solution.text: Positivity: xᵀMx = x₁² − 2x₁x₂ + 2x₂² = (x₁ − x₂)² + x₂² > 0 for x ≠ 0. Symmetry and linearity come from M = Mᵀ. ✓
What it tests: Any positive-definite symmetric M works (eigenvalues > 0). M = [1 −1; −1 1] would fail positivity.

parsons.goal: Prove: x̂ minimizes ‖b − Ax‖ if and only if AᵀAx̂ = Aᵀb.
lines: As x varies, Ax runs over all of Col A.
By the Best Approximation Theorem, ‖b − Ax‖ is smallest exactly when Ax = b̂ = proj<sub>Col A</sub> b.
Ax̂ = b̂ holds iff b − Ax̂ is orthogonal to Col A (orthogonal decomposition).
b − Ax̂ ⟂ Col A iff it is orthogonal to every column aⱼ, i.e. aⱼᵀ(b − Ax̂) = 0 for all j.

b − Ax̂ ⟂ Col A iff it is orthogonal to every row of A.

parsons.title: One step of Gram–Schmidt
parsons.goal: Show that v₂ = x₂ − (x₂·v₁/v₁·v₁)v₁ is orthogonal to v₁ and that Span{v₁, v₂} = Span{x₁, x₂} when v₁ = x₁.
lines: The factor v₁·v₁ cancels, giving v₂·v₁ = x₂·v₁ − x₂·v₁ = 0.
v₂ is a combination of x₂ and v₁ = x₁, so v₂ ∈ Span{x₁, x₂}.
Hence the two spans are equal. ∎
distractors: v₂ is a multiple of v₁, so the spans are equal.
